title: Atlas of Hegemony 1492–2010
metaDesc: An interactive world map of 16 moments from 1492 to 2010, layering the struggle for hegemony, who gained and lost from key events, and developments in technology and ideas.
subtitle: Over each year's borders: the struggle for hegemony · gains and losses · technology · ideas
hint: Colours show who ruled at that time, and each country has its own fixed colour. The stronger the colour, the firmer the rule; hatching means rule that is weakening or contested; a very pale colour means the country has left the contest for hegemony but still exists. Tap an area for its name and source; tap a country in the list below to keep only that country and follow its course and territory over time. ◆ marks strategic points such as straits, canals and bases; where the source map was wrong, the map has been recoloured with checked values.
footHtml: Borders: up to 1880, historical-basemaps (André Ourednik et al., GPL-3.0) with year-by-year corrections; from 1914, redrawn from CShapes 2.0 (Schvitz, Girardin, Weidmann et al., dated borders and colonies). For 1914 onwards, where both sources exist, the ‘Cross-check’ section of each year shows the agreement rate and where they differ. Strategic points and some regions were recoloured with checked values where the source was wrong. Territory areas are approximations computed by sampling the final map on a 0.25° grid. Because the gaps between years are uneven, ‘Gains and losses’ covers the main events since the previous year shown. Each year means ‘around then’, so events or works from a year or two later are sometimes included (e.g. the Navigation Act of 1651 under 1650). Small numbers in the text are footnotes on points where interpretations differ or a qualification is needed. For 1492–1880, places where the boundary itself was wrong (e.g. Iraq, Tunisia and Hungary in 1530; Qing Mongolia and the Amur basin in 1700) were found by comparing with the independent Cliopatria dataset (historical borders from the Seshat team); only those confirmed against the historical record were recoloured, borrowing Cliopatria’s boundary. The same corrections are applied to the companion world territory map. The two maps use different criteria, however: this atlas follows effective influence, colouring the British dominions (Canada, Australia, etc.) as British in 1914 and 1920, and Manchukuo and Ethiopia (1938) and Indonesia (1945) by the power actually in control, whereas the territory map follows legal sovereignty. Aragon in 1492 is shown as Spain here but as a separate state there, and the second-to-last year is 1994 here versus 1991 there.

ui.ckAbsentLong: The source border data does not draw this point (a small island or base). This marker is the checked value.
ui.ckDiffLong: ⚠ This differs from the map colour. The source border data draws this point as {map}. Small places such as bases and straits get swallowed by the surrounding area, or the source label is wrong — this marker is the checked value.
ui.ckMapNone: an area it does not draw
ui.trackAllNote: What has changed since the previous year shown. Tap a country to see its whole course. The status (rising, at its height, declining, etc.) is a judgement about international standing at the time, not about land area.
ui.trackNote: Tap a year to go to that map.
ui.trackBefore: Not treated as a contender on this map before {year}
ui.regionName: Name of the area at the time
ui.ckPatchedLong: In the source map this point was swallowed by the surrounding area or wrongly labelled, so the map itself has been recoloured with the checked ruler.
ui.vCs: Borders at this point were redrawn from CShapes 2.0 (as of {date}). Agreement with the open-source map used before (historical-basemaps): {agree}% (by area, 0.25° grid sample, coastline differences excluded). Strategic points and regions recoloured: {p}.
ui.vHb: Before 1886 there is no dated dataset to cross-check against. Based on historical-basemaps, {f} sovereignty-label errors were corrected and {p} strategic points and regions recoloured with checked values.
ui.vDiffs: Where the two sources differ most (source ↔ CShapes)
ui.vAdopt: Where they differ, the map follows CShapes.
ui.vExc: Shown differently from CShapes, or with a note added
ui.sparkNote: Areas are recomputed from what is coloured on this map (colonies included). Before 1886 they include nominal claims and spheres, so they can exceed real control.
ui.colorKeyNote: A country keeps the same colour even when its name changes (Russia → USSR → Russia, Ming → Qing → China). When it grows stronger or weaker, the colour stays and only its strength and hatching change.
ui.vClio: Before 1886 there is no date-level dataset, but great-power ownership was compared with the independent Cliopatria dataset. Agreement is {agree}% (share of cells, on a 0.5° grid, where both sources draw a state and assign it to the same great power). Based on historical-basemaps, {f} ownership errors were corrected and {p} strategic points and regions recoloured, {c} of them using boundaries borrowed from Cliopatria.
ui.vClioDiffs: Where the two still differ (this map ↔ Cliopatria)
ui.vClioNote: Most remaining differences come from how far nominal claims are coloured (the interior of Spanish America, Siberia) and how suzerainty is read (Egypt, Tibet, the Kazakh steppe). A difference does not mean this map is wrong, and Cliopatria has errors of its own. Places corrected with borrowed boundaries agree by construction.

glossary: Hegemony
The position of a state that sets the rules of the international order through military power, economic weight and institutions. This atlas colours the fifteen great powers that contested it.
historical-basemaps
An open dataset of world borders by period. The nine years up to 1880 come from it. It is volunteer-made, so precision varies by period.
CShapes 2.0
An academic dataset (ETH Zurich) recording, by date, the borders of independent states and their colonies and dependencies for 1886–2019. The seven years from 1914 come from it.
Cliopatria

A dataset of historical polity borders (3400 BCE–2024) published by the Seshat team. Here it is the comparison source for 1492–1880 and the source of boundaries borrowed to fix places where the border itself was wrong.
Cross-check
Comparing two independent sources to find where they disagree.
Agreement rate
The share of grid cells in which both sources assign the same great power. It is area-based and ignores coastline differences.
Recoloured
A place where the source was wrong or blank and the map was repainted with a checked value. Tap it to see why.
Strategic point (chokepoint)
A strait, canal or port so narrow that whoever holds it can control trade and military movement.
Nominal claim / sphere
Territory claimed by treaty or proclamation that actual administration did not reach. Maps before 1886 include such areas, so they can look larger than real control.
Suzerainty

A relationship in which one state leaves another's internal affairs alone but is acknowledged as its superior in diplomacy and war — the Ottomans with Egypt and the Crimean Khanate, the Qing with Tibet. Sources colour these differently.
Dominion

A member of the British Empire that governed itself internally while Britain decided its external relations (Canada, Australia, etc.). They became effectively independent with the Statute of Westminster (1931).
Protectorate / mandate / leased territory

A protectorate entrusts its diplomacy and defence to another state; a mandate is former enemy territory that the League of Nations assigned to a victor to administer after the First World War; a leased territory is land lent to another state for a fixed term.
